  • Can growth hormone injections make you taller after puberty?
Baby & Child

Can growth hormone injections make you taller after puberty?

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Advertisements for height-boosting injections can sound persuasive when you or your teenager wishes to be taller. Growth hormone is a real prescription treatment, but it is not a general height-enhancement product. The crucial questions are whether a medical indication exists and whether the skeleton still has growth remaining: not how confidently an advertisement promises extra centimetres.

Growth plates matter more than a birthday

Long bones become longer at growth plates near their ends. As skeletal maturation progresses, these areas fuse. Once they have closed, growth hormone cannot reopen them or restart lengthening of the long bones. Increasing the amount of hormone does not overcome that limit.

“After puberty” can be an imprecise phrase. Puberty is a process, and teenagers do not all mature on the same schedule. Turning eighteen or twenty is not a reliable test of whether growth remains. A clinician considers growth over time, puberty development and, when appropriate, a bone-age X-ray rather than relying on a universal age cutoff.

What determines a person’s height?

Height reflects many inherited genetic differences together with nutrition, health, hormonal function and the environment in which a child grows. Family heights offer useful context, but siblings can differ and a prediction is not a guarantee. Chronic illness or inadequate nutrition can also interfere with growth.

You may see the statement that height is “80% genetic.” Estimates of heritability describe variation across a studied population and environment; they do not divide an individual’s centimetres into a fixed genetic portion and a lifestyle portion. They also do not mean that the remaining percentage can be gained by buying a supplement or following a special routine.

Healthy habits support growth but do not bypass biology

Adequate food, sleep, appropriate activity and treatment of illness help support a child’s health and normal growth. Calcium and vitamin D matter for bone health, but taking extra supplements is not a proven way to add height beyond someone’s growth potential. Whether supplementation is needed depends on diet, age and medical advice.

Strength, posture and bone health remain worthwhile goals after growth has finished. Improving posture may change how someone stands, but it is different from lengthening mature bones. A programme that promises new adult height from stretching, exercise, diet or routine vitamin use should explain its evidence rather than treating those benefits as interchangeable.

What growth hormone actually does

Growth hormone, abbreviated GH or hGH, is produced by the pituitary gland at the base of the brain, close to the hypothalamus. It helps coordinate childhood growth, in part through insulin-like growth factor 1, or IGF-1. Prescription somatropin is a manufactured form used for defined indications.

Its actions extend beyond height to bone, muscle, body-fat distribution and the handling of sugar and fat. Deficiency can affect physical function and well-being, but tiredness, mood changes or a wish to gain muscle do not by themselves establish deficiency. A hormone having a normal role in the body does not mean that extra amounts improve that function.

Being short does not prove a hormone deficiency

Many shorter children are healthy. Some follow a family pattern of shorter adult height; others have constitutional delay, meaning that their growth and puberty mature later. A child who continues along a consistent growth curve is different from one whose growth rate slows unexpectedly.

A growth assessment looks at serial measurements, family history, birth history, nutrition and symptoms. Possible medical explanations include thyroid problems, chronic disease and particular genetic conditions as well as growth hormone deficiency. It is inaccurate to treat most short stature as a lack of GH, or to diagnose a growth disorder by comparison with classmates alone.

How a genuine deficiency can develop

Some people are born with genetic or structural differences affecting the pituitary region. Others develop a deficiency later after a tumour, surgery, radiation treatment or a significant brain injury. Certain infections, including meningitis, can damage this region too. Sometimes no specific cause is identified.

Not everyone with one of these experiences develops GH deficiency, and other pituitary hormones may also need assessment. Childhood-onset deficiency is not automatically a lifelong fixed condition in every case. The diagnosis, cause and continuing need for treatment should be reviewed as care moves from childhood into adulthood.

Testing needs specialist interpretation

A paediatric endocrinologist may review growth records, examine the child and request selected blood tests or a hand-and-wrist bone-age X-ray. Tests should answer a clinical question; not every healthy shorter child needs an extensive investigation. Bone age helps assess skeletal maturity but does not promise an exact future height.

GH is released in pulses, so a single random level cannot reliably diagnose deficiency. IGF-1 results also need interpretation in context. A stimulation test or pituitary imaging may be appropriate in selected cases. An online test package or one low result should not become a shortcut to self-prescribing injections.

Some childhood uses do not require GH deficiency

Approved uses differ by country and product. Selected children with growth problems associated with Turner syndrome, Prader-Willi syndrome or Noonan syndrome may be considered for treatment under particular prescribing criteria. These are different conditions; a diagnosis does not mean every affected child needs the same drug or has low GH.

For example, UK product information includes Turner-related growth disturbance and Prader-Willi growth/body-composition treatment for Genotropin, and Noonan-related growth failure for Norditropin. Other defined childhood indications also exist. This is why the blanket claim that GH is only ever used for deficiency is wrong, while specialist selection remains essential.

What appropriate childhood treatment involves

For an eligible child with remaining growth, treatment may improve growth rate and eventual adult height. The result depends on the diagnosis, when treatment begins, response, skeletal maturity and other health factors. No responsible plan can guarantee that a child will reach a preferred height or match another family member.

Treatment involves repeated injections and follow-up, sometimes over years. The family needs practical teaching about the prescribed product, administration and storage, plus a plan for missed doses and questions. The schedule is product-specific. Do not copy a regimen from another child or change the dose to chase a faster result.

Benefits, risks and follow-up belong in the same discussion

Established medical uses have evidence of benefit, but treatment is not risk-free and evidence differs across diagnoses. Monitoring can include growth response, IGF-1, thyroid function and glucose handling. The clinician also considers other medicines, pituitary hormone deficiencies and conditions that affect whether treatment is suitable.

Possible adverse effects include swelling, joint or muscle discomfort and injection-site problems. A severe or recurring headache with visual symptoms, a new limp, or persistent hip or knee pain needs prompt clinical advice. Breathing and sleep-related risks require particular attention in Prader-Willi syndrome. Ask for the warning signs that apply to the exact medicine and diagnosis.

The plan can change when growth finishes

When height growth is ending, the team should explain whether to stop height-directed treatment, reassess hormone function or continue replacement for another goal. Some people with childhood-onset isolated deficiency no longer meet criteria for adult treatment; others have persistent deficiency that still needs care.

Reassessment must be arranged by the treating team. Do not stop prescribed GH or other pituitary hormone medicines to perform your own experiment. Ask who will coordinate the transition to adult care, whether further tests are needed and how treatment success will be judged once centimetres are no longer the relevant measure.

Why some adults still receive growth hormone

Adults with confirmed, clinically significant deficiency may be considered for replacement. Potential benefits include body composition, bone health, exercise capacity and some measures of quality of life. Benefits and risks need individual assessment; treatment is not an automatic remedy for low energy or normal ageing.

Adult replacement does not demonstrate that injections can make mature bones longer. The treatment addresses a diagnosed endocrine problem with different objectives. Ask what improvement is expected in your case, how it will be measured and what findings would lead the team to adjust or reconsider treatment.

Excess hormone is not a route to extra adult height

Sustained excess GH in adults can enlarge soft tissues and alter bones of the hands, feet and face rather than increase height. Acromegaly, usually caused by a hormone-producing tumour, illustrates the effects of prolonged excess: changes in hand or shoe size, jaw or facial appearance, thicker skin and joint symptoms may occur.

Chronic excess can also contribute to problems with blood pressure, glucose regulation, the heart and breathing during sleep. That does not mean every prescribed injection causes these outcomes; dose, duration, diagnosis and supervision matter. It does explain why using unneeded GH, taking someone else’s medicine or escalating a dose is not a harmless height experiment.

Bring the concern to an appointment without making height a verdict

Bring previous measurements and ask whether the growth pattern is healthy, whether meaningful growth remains, and which diagnosis any treatment would address. Discuss expected benefit, uncertainty, costs, injection burden, monitoring and the plan when growth is complete. If a commercial clinic promises adult height gain, ask specifically how it determined growth-plate status and what evidence supports the claim.

A teenager’s distress about height is real even when no hormone treatment is indicated. Listen to concerns about teasing, confidence, sport or relationships and offer support without making a particular height the measure of success. Assessment should help the person understand their health, not make them feel responsible for achieving an advertised body size.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Growth-plate maturity determines whether longitudinal bone growth remains possible. Family height, growth velocity, puberty stage and selected investigations provide more useful context than a universal birthday cutoff.

Growth hormone has defined childhood and adult medical uses. Some childhood indications extend beyond deficiency, while adult replacement for confirmed deficiency has objectives other than height. Product approvals, contraindications and monitoring must be checked locally.

How BeMama can help

Keep earlier height measurements and write down the questions that matter to your family. Ask for an explanation of the growth pattern and the actual treatment goal before considering any injection, supplement or commercial height programme.

When to seek help

Use GH only through a qualified prescribing team. During treatment, promptly report severe or recurrent headache with visual changes, a new limp, persistent hip or knee pain, or breathing problems. Do not change prescribed hormone treatment on your own.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Closed growth plates cannot be reopened by taking more growth hormone.
  • A consistent shorter growth pattern may reflect healthy family variation or later maturation.
  • GH deficiency requires clinical assessment; a random hormone result is not enough.
  • Some products have additional childhood indications, with diagnosis-specific criteria.
  • Adult replacement can have health goals even though it cannot add height to mature bones.
  • A realistic care plan includes monitoring, uncertainty and support for body confidence.

Frequently asked questions

Can an eighteen-year-old still have growth remaining?

Possibly. Maturation varies, so age alone cannot answer it. A clinician can consider the growth record, puberty development and bone age when appropriate. Having growth remaining does not automatically make GH appropriate.

Can GH reopen closed growth plates?

No. Once growth plates are fused, extra GH does not restart lengthening of the long bones. Adult replacement for deficiency has different goals.

Does “80% genetic” mean I can improve the other 20%?

No. Heritability estimates describe differences across populations and environments, not a controllable percentage of one person’s height. Healthy habits support health without guaranteeing extra centimetres.

Should every shorter child be tested for GH deficiency?

No. Many are healthy and follow a family growth pattern or mature later. Growth over time and the clinical history help determine whether testing is needed.

Will calcium and vitamin D tablets make an adult taller?

They do not reopen mature growth plates. Adequate intake matters for bone health, and supplements may be advised for specific needs, but extra tablets are not a general adult-height treatment.

Is GH only prescribed when the body makes too little?

No. Some products have other approved childhood uses, including selected syndrome-related growth problems. Eligibility differs by diagnosis, medicine and country.

Does a Turner, Prader-Willi or Noonan diagnosis guarantee treatment?

No. The care team must consider the specific growth problem, local criteria, expected benefit and risks. Those conditions do not all have the same hormone profile or treatment plan.

Will childhood GH treatment necessarily continue for life?

No. Continuing need is reassessed as growth ends. Some people have persistent deficiency and others do not; the treating team should arrange the transition and any testing.

Why would an adult take GH if it cannot add height?

A person with confirmed deficiency may receive replacement for goals such as body composition, bone health or physical function. That is different from treating a healthy adult who wants to be taller.

Can I increase the dose if growth seems slow?

Do not change the dose yourself. Bring the measurements and concerns to the prescriber, who can review response, remaining growth, adherence and adverse effects without assuming that more hormone is better.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
